title: Past time expressions: cumulative review
objectives: Use common expressions for finished past time.
Choose prepositions for days, times and years.
Review past questions and actions in progress.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Time expressions help us say when something happened. We use yesterday for the day before today: ‘I worked yesterday’. We use last with expressions such as last night, last week, last month and last year: ‘They moved last year’. We can use ago after a length of time: ‘I saw her two days ago’. These expressions often accompany the past simple because they refer to a finished past time.

This unit also reviews past simple and past continuous forms. Use a past simple form for a finished event, and use was or were plus -ing to focus on an action in progress at a past time. The surrounding information helps us choose the form.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Use on before a named day: ‘on Monday’ or ‘on Friday morning’. Use at before a clock time: ‘at six’ or ‘at 8.30’. Use in before a year, a month or a part of the day: ‘in 2020’, ‘in April’ and ‘in the morning’. A common expression is at night. The context or a past verb can show that a named day or month is in the past.

Do not normally add a preposition before yesterday, last week or a time expression ending in ago: say ‘yesterday’, ‘last week’ and ‘three hours ago’. We can put many of these expressions at the end or the beginning of a sentence: ‘I called on Monday’ or ‘On Monday, I called’.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Look at the examples below. ‘I visited my aunt last Sunday’ describes a finished event. ‘At six last Sunday, I was travelling home’ focuses on an activity in progress at that time. In ‘I was travelling when she called’, the call is a past event that happened during the activity.

A time expression can be precise or general. ‘At half past seven’ gives a clock time; ‘last year’ gives a longer period. A long period does not automatically require the past continuous: ‘We lived there last year’ can present the situation as a completed past period. Choose according to the meaning.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not use last with ago: say ‘two days ago’, not ‘last two days ago’. The phrase ‘the last two days’ exists, but it has a different form and can be used in a different time context. Also distinguish yesterday morning from last night; ‘yesterday night’ is generally unusual in standard British English.

With ordinary past simple verbs, use did and the base verb in questions: ‘Did you work yesterday?’ With be, use was or were: ‘Were you at home yesterday?’ With the past continuous, use was or were plus -ing: ‘Were you working at six?’ These are different patterns, even when the same time expression appears.

examples.note: Yesterday means the day before today.
Last month names a finished past month.
Ago follows the length of time.
Use on with a named day.
Use at with a clock time.

examples.sentence: At eight last night, we were studying.
examples.note: Were studying focuses on progress at eight.

examples.sentence: I was reading when the lights went out.
examples.note: The past event happened during the activity in progress.

common_errors.reason: Do not use in before yesterday in this pattern.
Use at with a clock time.

common_errors.incorrect: She left two days before ago.
common_errors.reason: Ago follows the length of time without before.

summary: Use yesterday, last week and expressions such as two days ago for past time.
Use on with days, at with clock times and in with years and months.
Choose past simple or past continuous according to the situation being described.
